1:4.t: "Grace, mercy and peace": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "Grace and peace". "God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ": many early manuscripts read "God the Father and Christ Jesus".

1:5.t: Crete: the large island south of Greece. Paul passed it on his voyage to Rome (Acts 27:7-13); this visit was probably after his release.

1:7.t: "Overseer": the KJV's "bishop". The same men are called elders in 1:5; see Acts 20:28.

1:12.t: The saying is attributed to Epimenides, a Cretan poet of the sixth century BC (compare Acts 17:28).

2:5.t: "Busy at home": the KJV's "keepers at home".

3:12.t: Nicopolis was probably the city of that name on the west coast of Greece.

2:13.t: "Our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ" (Greek tou megalou theou kai soteros hemon Iesou Christou): the KJV's "the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ". Greek grammar (one article governing both nouns) most naturally reads both titles as referring to Jesus. The KJV wording allows either reading.

2:14.t: "A people that are His very own" (Greek laon periousion): the KJV's "a peculiar people", which in 1611 meant a people belonging especially to Him (Exodus 19:5, Deuteronomy 7:6), not an odd people.

3:5.t: "The washing of rebirth" (Greek loutrou palingenesias): the KJV's "the washing of regeneration". See Matthew 19:28. Christians understand this as baptism, or as the inner cleansing that baptism signifies, and both as the work of the Holy Spirit.

3:10.t: "Divisive person" (Greek hairetikon anthropon): the KJV's "an heretick", one who causes factions. See Acts 24:14.
